thread.title: Invest In Liberty Sirius Class A? Yes. But Not Just Yet - Liberty Sirius XM Series A (NASDAQ:LSXMA)

author: Max Greve
title: Invest In Liberty Sirius Class A? Yes. But Not Just Yet - Liberty Sirius XM Series A (NASDAQ:LSXMA)
text:
With the results of the merger vote officially in at Pandora ( P ), the company is officially set to be acquired by Sirius XM ( SIRI ) in the very near future. I remain convinced that Pandora sold low and was already on the path to profitability on its own, and that its shareholders will now have to share their upside unnecessarily. But that is no longer here nor there. With the company officially a historical one only now, I want to take a quick look at the new undervalued stock in the streaming audio space. No, not Sirius XM, Liberty Sirius XM ( LSXMA ). With Pandora under its belt it is now clearly in an advantageous position in the industry, and I might well be inclined to recommend opening a long position. But, I don’t recommend it just yet .
A Discounted Entry Point As Contributors Crunching Numbers and Belgian Dentist have already noted , Liberty Sirius XM, which owns a roughly 72% stake in Sirius XM, trades at a substantial discount to the valuation implied by the price of the underlying asset. Therefore, while someone could conceivably be bullish on Liberty Sirius XM without being bullish on Sirius XM proper, it is hard to see how anyone could rationally take the opposite view. Most, of course, are bullish on both. For myself I see the question of Sirius XM’s ultimate value to be a slightly closer question, so I am appreciative of the extra margin of safety a Liberty investment provides.
I also appreciate voting rights commensurate with my investment. Liberty Sirius XM is actually divided into three classes of stock, with the superpowered voting rights concentrated in the class B shares. B shares are approximately 3% of the float, but have one-third the voting rights. Almost all of the group B shares are owned by Liberty’s board of directors, however.
Meanwhile, group A shares carry 100x more voting power than group C shares, so they are still overweight in the vote count. They represent approximately one-third the total float and carry approximately one-half of the total voting power, so they are still a stock that treats its holder fairly at voting time. So group A shares are the focus of this article.
Watching The Float Now, on to the numbers proper. First, let me explain why I am still in favor of waiting a little longer before buying into Liberty.
Pandora currently has some 273 million shares outstanding, each of which is about to be translated into 1.44 shares of Sirius XM stock. That stock, in turn, currently has 4.4 billion shares outstanding, about to become close to 4.8 billion. This is good news for Liberty, since it means Liberty will see only a small dilution in its total stockholdings - from 72% down to roughly 67%.
However , because the vast majority of those shares are owned by Liberty, they aren’t really trading in the market since Liberty is not looking to reduce its stake. That means that the float of Sirius XM shares is closer to 1.2 billion right now. With Pandora’s shareholders all being outside of Liberty as well, the float is about to increase to 1.6 billion, taking the full brunt of the share increase. That is a 33% increase in shares actually trading in the market.
Thus, analyzing Sirius XM’s share price and stock on its own can lead us to under-appreciate just how much trading in that stock could be impacted by the new shares about to be issued. If Pandora shareholders look to cash out after the merger goes through, rather than holding their shares, they can put outsized selling pressure on the Sirius stock due to the relatively small float.
Assuming Liberty maintains its discount, which has existed for quite a while now, it could potentially follow Sirius down and offer a better entry point in a few weeks' time.
A Sirius Risk Of course, that is only a consideration if Pandora’s former shareholders don’t want to hold Sirius. As I said, most are bullish on Sirius right now, because it offers large cash flow that it can use to fund the new digital radio pioneer it just acquired in its battle with Apple ( AAPL ) and Spotify ( SPOT ).
The problem here is, satellite technology is a great way to be rich today and poor tomorrow. This is because it is hands down the hardest of the legacy media technologies to transition to 21 st -century digital delivery of media. I explored this issue at length a few years ago when I raised deep concerns about AT&T’s ( T ) purchase of DIRECTV. Needless to say, that has not worked out as well as AT&T would have liked. I won’t repeat the entire argument here, but suffice to say that Sirius XM’s free cash flow, as attractive as it is now, does not seem to me to be especially secure as wireless terrestrial technology (cell carriers) increasingly supplants wireless satellite technology.
Liberty And Sirius Which brings me back to Liberty. Liberty offers a substantial discount to Sirius XM’s shares. Each share is worth just under 10 Sirius XM shares, which should put it at almost $60 as of this writing. And yet it trades for under $40.
This is an entry price I am far more comfortable with. It is essentially a way to price in the decline I see as a major risk to Sirius’s existing satellite-based cash flow. I have explored the radio market in several articles over the years, so I have provided links to them and will only summarize the key points here.
Sirius XM is currently generating almost $900 million in profits off of strong operating leverage in its high fixed-cost satellite system. But it is helped in this regard by lower content costs than digital players - still higher than terrestrial radio, though, which pays nothing - and it is also vulnerable to that very same operating leverage being unwound and becoming a drag if subscribers start to leave for other technologies in any significant numbers. Witness what is currently happening to DIRECTV.
Financial Calculations To be conservative, we will assume that Sirius’s satellite income will eventually fade to half of current levels, and Pandora will have to carry the other half. That’s almost certainly far too pessimistic, but again, conservative. At $40 per share, Sirius XM/Pandora combined need to generate approximately $960 million annually in profit to justify an investment in Liberty at a 20 P/E.
Pandora is the leading, and I have long argued, really the only player in digital radio advertising, which has a current market of $16-17 billion. At the low end, Pandora would need to clear 30% margins on 10% of that market to achieve its half. How feasible is that? Considering Pandora already accounts for close to 10% of total listenership and generates gross margins of 30-35%, I’d say very. This is before considering all the users of Sirius’s satellites who can be transitioned to Pandora’s platform rather than a competitor’s when they leave the satellite ecosystem. Those add-ons should more than cover Pandora’s fixed costs like G&A and product development.
Meanwhile, Sirius’s own shareholders need the combo to generate an additional $480 million in profit to achieve the same benchmark. So they basically need Sirius’s satellite cash flow to not shrink at all, while Pandora hits all the same benchmarks. That seems to me a good deal more questionable, which is why I am wary of a direct Sirius investment.
Summary The merger deal is probably bullish for Sirius shares as well, but it is even more bullish for Liberty shares. While Sirius itself still makes me nervous, the discount Liberty trades at will probably be enough to put me over the top. In a little while longer, after the fallout from the merger has cleared a bit.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions.
